newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Gum arabic producers fail to form cartel.
newsitem.headline: Gum arabic producers fail to form cartel.

text.p: African producers of gum arabic who were expected to set up a body to advance their interests failed to do so at a conference ending in Lagos on Friday, delegates to the meeting said.
They said only four of the seven nations expected attended.
"A steering committee was set up to prepare for the next meeting to be held in Sudan," said Chidume Okoro, the Nigerian spokesman and chief convener of the producers' meeting.
Nigeria, Chad, Sudan and Niger attended the Lagos meeting while Senegal, Mali and Mauritania were absent.

The seven African countries jointly produce the estimated world output of 55,000 metric tonnes per annum, almost all of which is shipped to developed countries for processing into industrial raw material.
The commodity, otherwise known as Acacia Senegalese, is used widely in the food, soft drink, pharmaceuticals, confectionery, textile, printing and cosmetics industries.
Most industries use it as a stabilising agent. While manufacturers of drugs use it to coat tablets, breweries and food firms use it as a preservative.
Nigeria is the second biggest producer, behind Sudan, with an output of 5,000 tonnes and one billion naira ($12.5 million) income annually.
The producers charged at the Lagos conference that importers from the developed countries were arbitrarily dictating the international price of gum arabic.
"Today the official price of this raw material is $2,200 down from $6,000 which was the price a few years ago," said Okoro.
But Okoro, whose company Tradacon is a major exporter from Nigeria, said African producers had not helped the situation by what he called their "undesirable activities."
These included price undercutting, large scale over-production, poor quality control, lack of support from governments and lack of cooperation among producing nations, he added.
